title: The boy in the poisoned pool
hookLine: a poisoned pool, a boy wrapped in a serpent's coils, a weeping village, and one brother smiling
carry: lila: what looks like danger is his play
tomorrow: The dance on the serpent's hoods

lines: A HOT DAY BY THE YAMUNA.
cards: A hot day by the Yamuna. The boy Krishna is old enough now to take the calves and cows out to graze with his friends. Balarama isn't with them today.
Desperate with thirst, the boys and the cattle drink from the river, and drop where they stand, lifeless at the water's edge.
Krishna looks at them, the text says, with a glance full of nectar, and they get up, puzzled, as if waking from sleep. Something is wrong with that water.

teach.h: A POISONED POOL IN THE YAMUNA.
teach.b: What's wrong is Kaliya. In a deep pool of the Yamuna lives a great serpent, a naga with many hoods, whose poison has made the pool boil. Birds flying over it, the Bhagavata says, fall out of the sky.
Krishna decides the river has to be clean again.

teach.h: HE JUMPS FROM THE KADAMBA TREE.
teach.b: He climbs a tall kadamba tree on the bank, tightens his clothes, slaps his arms like a wrestler, and jumps into the poisoned pool.
Kaliya rises, furious, sees a small, dark, beautiful boy playing in his water, bites him, and wraps him in his coils. And Krishna goes still.
The whole village runs to the river, even the cows, and sees him, motionless, wrapped in a serpent. The mothers weep around Yashoda. Nanda and the men start toward the water to go in after him.
One person on that bank is calm.
Balarama, the text says, smiles and says nothing, because he knows his brother's power. Then he holds them back. Why smile?
Because he knows who is in the water.

Hindus have a word for everything Krishna does in Vraja: lila, divine play. As devotees read it, a Lord who can't be harmed lets himself look caught, and the people who love him show how much they love him.
The village's fear isn't silly; their love is the point. But the one they're grieving is not lost.
That's why devotees still act these stories out as Krishna lila, plays where everyone on the bank already knows the ending, and still gasps.
And many devotees carry this into their own hard nights: the worry is real, like Yashoda's, and so is Balarama's trust that Krishna holds the ending.

how: Pilgrims in Vrindavan visit Kaliya Ghat on the Yamuna, and in Varanasi the Nag Nathaiya festival reenacts the leap: a boy playing Krishna jumps into the river and rises standing on the serpent.

o: the boy's friend who drinks first from the pool
the many-hooded serpent whose poison fills a river pool
the kadamba tree Krishna jumps from into the pool

games.q: the poisoned pool — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna falls into the pool by accident
he climbs the kadamba tree and jumps in on purpose.
the boys who drank the water are revived by Krishna's glance
they get up as if waking from sleep.
Balarama smiles because he doesn't care
he smiles because he knows his brother's power. Hindus call Krishna's deeds lila, divine play.

games.q: you're watching a Krishna lila play by a river. the boy playing Krishna jumps in and lies still in the serpent's coils. the old woman beside you smiles. why?
o: she thinks the boy is a bad actor.
she knows the story: it's lila, and Krishna is never really caught.
she's glad the play is almost over.
games.why: like Balarama on the bank, devotees know who's in the water. Krishna's deeds are lila, divine play.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love who is in a hard place, someone you can only watch from the bank. Breathe with the worry; Yashoda's fear was real.
Then, if you pray, say their name and Krishna's together, softly, a few times, as many Hindus do when someone they love is in danger, leaning on what Balarama knew.
If you don't pray, hold them in your mind, one steady breath at a time.

wordCard.voice: Kaliya. The many-hooded serpent whose poison fills a pool of the Yamuna, and who wraps the boy Krishna in his coils.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kaliya, the serpent of the Yamuna pool.
